did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title attributes it to David and identifies it as a psalm intended for the director of music. From the very beginning, David addresses the Lord with the words, “O God whom I praise, do not remain silent.”
The brief phrase “But I am prayer” expresses David’s response to his enemies’ hatred: instead of answering hatred with hatred, he turns to the Lord in prayer.
David describes a painful moral reversal: his enemies repay him with “evil for good” and “hatred for love.”

From this verse through verse 20, the psalm uses language of curses and requests for punishment: condemnation in court, a shortened life, harm to the family and possessions, and the erasure of his memory.

In the description of the punishment, the people connected with the wicked man are said to “wander about” and seek their needs among the ruins of their homes; the image emphasizes the loss of home and stability.

The psalm gives the reason for the curse in the words, “because he did not remember to show kindness”: the wicked man is portrayed as persecuting the poor, the needy, and the brokenhearted instead of treating them with kindness.

The curse is described through three vivid images: like a garment a person wears, like water entering his body, and like oil penetrating his bones. These images emphasize that the curse surrounds him and penetrates him.

Beginning with verse 21, the direction of the psalm changes: after describing the curses, David returns to addressing the Lord directly and asks for deliverance “for the sake of your name” and because of his steadfast love.
David describes himself as “poor and needy” and as one whose heart is “wounded within him,” presenting both his physical and emotional condition as part of his plea for deliverance.
David expresses confidence in a reversal of fortunes: the enemies may curse, but the Lord will bless; therefore, they will be put to shame, while the Lord’s servant will rejoice.

The psalm ends by emphasizing public thanksgiving: David promises to give thanks and praise to the Lord “in the midst of many,” because the Lord stands at the right hand of the needy and saves him from those who condemn him.
